events.action: Speed up patching, enable automatic updates where suitable and check suppliers can fix systems they manage quickly. Cut internet exposure, enforce MFA, retire unsupported systems, monitor for suspicious activity and use temporary controls where a fix must wait.
events.exec: The national cyber agency is telling Australian organisations to plan for shorter patch windows and more frequent emergency updates.
events.plain: Australia's cyber agency warns that hackers now exploit new software flaws within days, so organisations must install security updates much faster.

key_findings: The ACSC circulated a critical alert on November 17 urging organisations to patch, protect and prevent.
Publicly reported vulnerabilities rose 30 per cent over the 2025-26 financial year, per the agency's Annual Cyber Threat Report.
Some compromises occurred within 48 hours of security updates being published.
The alert addresses the overall pace of disclosure and exploitation rather than one product or flaw.
recommendations: Patch faster, turn on automatic updates where suitable and make sure suppliers can quickly fix systems they manage.
Cut unnecessary internet-facing exposure, tighten identity and access controls including MFA, and deal with legacy or unsupported systems.
Monitor for suspicious activity and fix known vulnerabilities before attackers use them.
If an update cannot be applied at once, assess the risk, restrict exposure and apply temporary controls.

events.summary: The ACSC issued a critical alert on November 17 warning that vulnerabilities are being disclosed faster, updates are arriving more often and some compromises occur within 48 hours of a patch being published. events.action: Remove default or hardcoded credentials (including the LiteLLM default master key), require login on AI gateways and builders, patch Langflow and RAGFlow, rotate keys ever exposed in code, and watch for unexpected AI spend or usage.
events.exec: Exposed AI gateways are being mined for provider keys by automated agents; stolen keys mean unexpected bills and wider cloud access.
events.plain: Amazon says AI agents, likely run by China-linked groups, scanned the internet for poorly secured AI tools to steal the access keys inside them, and separately tried to fool identity checks at crypto exchanges with deepfake video.

key_findings: Between October 3 and November 5 Amazon saw two campaigns it assesses, with moderate confidence, used ARTEX agents run by disparate Chinese-nexus groups.
Campaign 1 found exposed AI gateways and builders (One API, LiteLLM, Dify, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI and others), extracted upstream provider keys, validated and pooled them.
Stolen keys funded the model gateway driving further key hunting; agents also used CVE-2025-3248, CVE-2026-28797, a One API header bypass and the LiteLLM default master key.
Campaign 2 attacked identity verification at two crypto exchanges with real-time deepfake video and forged ID photos; the vendor rejected every recorded attempt.
Amazon did not watch the activity live and could not verify the agents' reported outcomes; it publishes 11 IP indicators.
recommendations: Fix basics: default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code or public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and unpatched software.
Assume exposed secrets and misconfigurations will be found quickly and remediate on that basis.
Put AI apps, model gateways and inference endpoints under the same controls as other production systems.
Watch for misuse through unexpected spend or unusual usage.

events.summary: Amazon observed two campaigns between October 3 and November 5 that it assesses, with moderate confidence, were run with ARTEX AI agents by Chinese-nexus groups. One hunted internet-exposed AI gateways and app builders for upstream provider keys; the other tried to beat identity checks at two crypto exchanges with real-time deepfake video and forged ID photos. One vendor's server rejected every deepfake attempt the agents recorded.
events.title: Amazon uncovers AI agent campaign hunting exposed apps for AI provider keys

events.action: Renew any authentication secret that is or may be compromised, enforce strong authentication and tight control of privileged accounts, filter access to block bulk extraction, and test internet-facing applications for IDOR flaws.
events.exec: The French state's own post-mortem shows stolen credentials, weak sign-in and simple web flaws, not novel exploits, driving public-sector data loss.
events.plain: France's cyber agency says 64 new data breaches reached it since September 30, five at ministries or their agencies. Known causes: stolen passwords, accounts without a second sign-in step, or web pages that exposed other people's files.

key_findings: 64 new data violations were reported since the September 30 report; five concern ministries or subordinate bodies and are handled with ANSSI support.
New cases: about 1.2 million CAF/VACAF case files, over 60,000 France Travail agents and professionals, 30,500 ASP DEFI users, over 1,000 OFB permit users, about 100 foreign ministry library users.
25 of 30 education academies had incidents between July and September 2026; intruders reused valid credentials and moved across the interministerial state network.
Every breach used weaknesses already seen: missing or weak MFA, infostealer-compromised accounts, subcontractor exposure, IDOR flaws and configuration defects.
At France Travail a compromised agent account, with second-factor (SMS) validation, allowed exfiltration; elsewhere MFA stopped logins with stolen VPN certificates.
recommendations: Immediately renew authentication secrets that are compromised or suspected to be.
Enforce strong authentication everywhere and strictly control privileged accounts.
Harden access filtering to prevent data exfiltration.
Strengthen security of internet-exposed applications and those linked to third-party networks.
Notify affected people where the nature of the data requires it.

events.summary: CERT-FR's second REACTIV situation report counts 64 new data violations since September 30, five of them at ministries or their agencies: a foreign ministry library portal, the OFB permit portal, France Travail (over 60,000 agents and professionals), CAF's VACAF (about 1.2 million case files) and the ASP DEFI portal (30,500 users). ANSSI found no new weakness types: missing multi-factor sign-in, infostealer-stolen accounts, supplier exposure and IDOR flaws recur.
events.title: ANSSI's second REACTIV report details October data leaks across French state bodies

recommendations: Where a flaw cannot be fixed in 30 or 45 days, Anthropic says it will work with the vendor on a remediation timeline.

events.title: Apache warns Roller RCE flaw (CVE-2026-129448) is exploited in attacks
events.summary: Apache says an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in Roller, CVE-2026-129448, is being exploited. It is a deserialization bug in the XML-RPC interface affecting versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4, and is the same bug as CVE-2026-82384, which named only 6.1.5. Version 6.1.6 or later fixes it.
events.plain: Apache says attackers are already exploiting a flaw that lets anyone run code on servers running Roller, its blogging software.
events.exec: An exploited unauthenticated flaw in internet-facing blog servers; fix exists.
events.action: Upgrade Apache Roller to 6.1.6 or later. If you cannot, Apache's workaround is to set enabledForExtensions to false in WEB-INF/web.xml or remove the /roller-services/xmlrpc mapping (reports differ on whether both are needed), then restart; switching off XML-RPC in the admin UI is not enough.

key_findings: Unauthenticated RCE through XML-RPC deserialization in Roller 4.0.0 to 6.1.4; Apache says it is exploited.
Same bug as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only 6.1.5.
Fixed in 6.1.6; a configuration workaround is given.
recommendations: Upgrade to 6.1.6 or apply the web.xml workaround.

validation.note: Compared BleepingComputer with The Hacker News (separate reporting of the ASF statement): CVE-2026-129448, versions 4.0.0-6.1.4, ASF says actively exploited, fix 6.1.6, web.xml workaround, CVSS 9.8 all agree. Attackers and victim counts not disclosed.

key_findings: Rapid7 MDR detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against a customer's Confluence Data Center on November 13; a public proof of concept targeting N-able N-central had been published on November 12.

recommendations: Upgrade Confluence Data Center to 9.2.28 or a current 10.x release, internet-facing systems first.

Upgrade N-central to 2026.4 HF3 (2026.4.1.39) and confirm the Legacy API is disabled.
Investigate exposed systems for signs of compromise using the indicators Rapid7 published.

events.action: Hunt for the published EggStreme indicators, restrict built-in tools such as WScript and cmd to roles that need them, inventory unmanaged machines reachable over SMB, and alert on new inbound listeners such as TCP 5060 on workstations.
events.exec: A suspected China-linked espionage toolkit is being rebuilt to avoid beacon-based detection, so networks that rely on outbound traffic alerts may miss it.
events.plain: Security firm Bitdefender says a spy toolkit it first found in 2025 has been reworked and is still used against several Philippine government bodies, and it now hides better.

key_findings: Bitdefender assesses with high confidence that the operation still targets multiple Philippine government organisations, and with low to medium confidence Taiwan; the page does not publish a victim count.

EggStreme is a multi-stage fileless framework; the newer agent uses raw TCP wrapped in mutual TLS plus an AES-256-CBC layer instead of gRPC and has no keylogger, and passive-mode builds do not beacon out but listen on TCP 5060.
The Fuel configuration moved from RC4 to AES-256-CBC and the loader moved to custom ciphers, with two variants dated from 28 October and mid-December 2025.

Operators moved laterally by staging a Fuel package and VBS scripts on an unmanaged host reachable over SMB; the page says valid credentials and a reachable share were enough on multiple machines, and does not state the initial access vector.
Attribution is unchanged: a suspected Chinese APT group, which the page says is not a statement about any government's involvement.
recommendations: Restrict built-in tools such as WScript.exe, cmd.exe, reg.exe and attrib.exe to roles that need them.
Detect DLL sideloading by system-library name and load location using runtime behavioural monitoring, not signatures.
Inventory unmanaged assets that reach workstations over SMB and watch SMB-launched scripts.
Baseline host firewall rules and alert on new inbound listeners such as TCP 5060 on workstations.
Detect CLR and in-process PowerShell loading in non-.NET processes and capture PowerShell script block logging.

report.doc_id: How AI Agents Become New Targets in GitHub Malware Campaign
key_findings: Researcher Andrei Anton-Aanei identified 22 malicious GitHub links with files designed to make AI-assisted tools execute a concealed payload.
Instruction files describe setup.js as a sealed, signed artifact and tell the assistant not to read it and to run it without confirmation.
A second path uses session-start hooks in project settings such as .claude/settings.json, which can run a command once the developer trusts the repository.
Bitdefender describes setup.js as a multistage loader that can steal source-control, cloud, CI/CD and package-registry credentials, and modify agent configurations for 14 coding tools.
Stolen GitHub or GitLab access can be used to plant malicious files in other repositories and attempt to republish infected packages.
recommendations: Review agent instruction files, startup hooks, MCP definitions and editor tasks before granting an unfamiliar workspace trust.
If execution is suspected, isolate the workstation and revoke exposed tokens from a clean system.

events.summary: Bitdefender Labs says it found 22 malicious GitHub links whose instruction files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md tell AI coding assistants to run a setup.js loader without inspecting it, while other files use session-start hooks to run it directly. events.action: Upgrade CAST Imaging to a newer version than 3.6.2 as the vendor advises, and restrict network access to the Imaging web interface and its Keycloak endpoints until patched.
events.exec: Software used to map application architecture has flaws that let outsiders impersonate administrators or read files; unpatched installs expose internal code analysis data.
events.geo_basis: vendor headquarters (not stated in source; CAST Software is based in Paris)
events.plain: CERT Polska reports several security flaws in CAST Imaging, software that analyses application code. Some let attackers pose as administrators or read files. The vendor says newer versions fix them.

key_findings: CERT Polska lists eight CVEs (CVE-2026-109857 to CVE-2026-109864) in CAST Imaging; only version 3.6.2 is confirmed affected and other versions may be too.
CVE-2026-109857: the TenantFilter class trusts the X-ISSUER-LOCATION header, allowing administrator impersonation.

events.action: Enforce MFA on all remote access, keep firewalls and VPN appliances patched and their management interfaces off the internet, hold offline immutable backups, and alert on Defender being disabled, logs cleared or WinSCP moving data out.
events.exec: A national agency profile of an active ransomware service; remote access without MFA and exposed management interfaces are its way in.
events.plain: India's cyber agency published a warning about The Gentlemen, a criminal group that rents out ransomware. It breaks in through remote-access equipment or stolen passwords, copies data, then locks Windows, Linux and virtual servers.

key_findings: The Gentlemen is a financially motivated ransomware-as-a-service group using double extortion; its Go-based payload is obfuscated with Garble and can self-propagate.
It targets Windows, Linux, BSD, NAS devices and VMware ESXi; reported sectors include healthcare, construction, finance and manufacturing.
Initial access is through internet-facing edge devices, RDP and VPN services, or compromised credentials.
Operators spread through Group Policy Objects and the NETLOGON share, disable Microsoft Defender, delete shadow copies and clear event and RDP logs.
Data is exfiltrated with WinSCP before encryption; the advisory lists file hashes, IP addresses and domains but no CVEs.
recommendations: Inventory internet-facing services, disable those not needed and keep management interfaces off the public internet.
Patch firewalls and VPN appliances and enforce MFA for all remote access.
Keep offline, encrypted, immutable backups isolated from production and test restoration.
Review Group Policy Objects, domain admin membership and changes to NETLOGON and SYSVOL regularly.
Do not pay ransoms; report incidents to CERT-In and law enforcement.

events.plain: Check Point says attackers broke into about two dozen of its security devices that lacked a fix issued on October 23. Some Israeli organisations had data wiped; later attacks in other countries were not destructive.

key_findings: Attackers used PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVSS 9.2) in the Mobile Access Portal for unauthenticated code execution, then CVE-2026-123039 to become root.
Exploitation began October 30, about a week after the PHP2Shell hotfix of October 23; the advisory counts a couple of dozen compromised unpatched systems.
The first wave targeted Israeli organisations and was destructive in a limited number of cases; a second wave from November 2 reached organisations in several countries with no destruction reported.
Tools included the TSGA backdoor, a TSProxy library, PHP webshells, a network scanner and a wiper that was also run on a VMware ESXi host reached over SSH.
Check Point Research links the tooling to the PhiliKit framework but does not attribute the campaign with confidence and raises a possible false flag.

Contact Check Point Support for exposure assessment; absence of an indicator match does not rule out compromise.

key_findings: Dorsett Controls InfoScan 1.45.0 and earlier is affected; it is deployed worldwide in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector.
CVE-2026-117659 (CVSS 8.1): the Electron desktop client accepts TLS certificates without validation and runs with insecure settings, so traffic can be intercepted or altered.
Unauthenticated endpoints and the public installer reveal usernames, MFA status, version and firmware details, the BACnet/IP port and customer and internal hostnames.
Hard-coded cryptographic keys protect the MongoDB password kept in the Windows registry, so it may be recoverable.
CISA reports no known public exploitation; the vendor fix is dated October 22, 2026.
recommendations: Upgrade to InfoScan v1.46 or later, online through System Maintenance or offline from the Dorsett Controls Customer Portal.
Keep control system devices and systems off the internet.
Place control networks and remote devices behind firewalls, separated from business networks.
Use up-to-date VPNs for remote access.
Report suspected malicious activity to CISA.

events.action: Apply Talos's guidance: alert on unusually rapid activity, enforce MFA and rate limits against password spraying, turn on EDR tamper protection, remove exposed secrets, limit privileges, and deploy the listed Snort and ClamAV coverage.

events.plain: Cisco Talos says AI-driven hacking tools such as ARTEX are now used by spies and criminals alike, and counted over 2,500 internet addresses tied to ARTEX and over 700 PentAGI control panels reachable online.

key_findings: Talos counted more than 2,500 ARTEX-associated C2 IP addresses and more than 700 reachable PentAGI instances.
The platforms automate the full chain from reconnaissance to follow-on actions; one cited case went from a GitHub search to Azure Key Vault exfiltration within five minutes.
Entry methods seen include password spraying, exposed or stolen credentials, long-term AWS keys and web flaws such as missing API authentication and injection.
Cited activity: VAPOR PANDA against more than 200 organisations in at least 14 countries since October 17, and Storm-0940 reaching more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants.
Both state-aligned and financially motivated groups use the tools, including a Cambodia-based group deploying VShell and AdaptixC2 in Southeast Asia.
recommendations: Monitor for rapid, machine-speed activity and prepare fast containment.
Defend against credential attacks with MFA, rate limits and password-spray alerts.
Harden EDR with tamper protection and harden public-facing systems.
Remove exposed secrets, limit privileges and secure cloud resources.
Deploy the Snort rules and ClamAV signatures Talos lists for ARTEX, AdaptixC2, VShell and FScan.

events.action: Stop using static, non-expiring credentials in CI/CD pipelines and put IP restrictions and rate limits on API tokens. Require hardware security keys, enable rate limiting and bot defence, and end every ruleset with a default-deny rule.
events.exec: Automated AI scanning is now routine background traffic; long-lived keys without restrictions are what turns scanning into a breach.
events.plain: Cloudflare says automated AI hacking tools are scanning its customers about 30 times more than in early October, and that long-lived access keys with no restrictions gave attackers their way in.

key_findings: More than 50 AI pentesting framework families tried to scan Cloudflare customers in a three-day window, from thousands of IP addresses.
Daily requests from these tools rose about 30-fold since October 1 and more than tenfold after the original ARTEX repository was removed on October 8.
ARTEX and its forks are over 60% of tracked orchestrators; the ecosystem has more than 12,000 repositories.
In one incident a compromised account-level API token with no IP restriction or rate limit allowed 400 database dump requests in an hour.
Other intruders pivoted from a hyperscaler environment into customer environments using static, non-expiring CI/CD tokens.
recommendations: Stop relying on static, non-expiring credentials in CI/CD pipelines.
Deploy a WAF with rate limiting and run anomaly detection on all customer-facing web applications.
Enforce API schema validation, mTLS and a default-deny rule at the end of every ruleset.
Require identity-gated access for high-risk apps and hardware-based FIDO security keys.
Use bot defence and challenges to identify automated agents.

events.action: Confirm technician clients run ScreenConnect 26.6.5 or later, disable RMM+ extension 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, review Run Command history, and check endpoints for a second ScreenConnect client. Do not connect to suspect hosts through ScreenConnect.
events.exec: Hundreds of managed endpoints were hit through a faulty third-party add-on; the feared spread to IT providers' own machines has not been observed.
events.plain: Attackers pushed fake copies of ConnectWise ScreenConnect remote-support software to hundreds of computers. Their toolkit tries to steal the login session cookie of any IT technician who connects to an infected machine, but researchers have not seen that step work.

key_findings: Huntress saw rogue ScreenConnect clients pushed to at least 288 hosts at 48 organisations on November 11 and 205 hosts at 41 organisations in a second wave on November 13.
Operators used the Run Command feature on cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to run commands as SYSTEM; one panel alone reached 190 downstream clients.
Entry appears tied to the third-party RMM+ extension, versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, which accepted a blank access key; ConnectWise disabled five extensions across about 400 partner environments.

SCKit is 16 scripts and config files that install a rogue client, hijack the real client's connection and try to steal the technician's .aspxauth session cookie (and browser cookie stores) to replay against the panel. Huntress describes CVE-2026-84869 (client flaw before 26.6.5) as background, not as the method SCKit uses.
Huntress has not seen the jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation succeed in any recovered log.
recommendations: Verify every technician client runs ScreenConnect 26.6.5 or later and disable the affected RMM+ extension versions.
Review Run Command and Toolbox history for unexpected mass activity and check endpoints for a second, unauthorised ScreenConnect client.
Do not connect to a suspected host through ScreenConnect; use WinRM or another out-of-band tool and isolate it until cleaned.
Remove the rogue client service, the TrapWatch scheduled task and the RelayTrap folder, then rotate ScreenConnect credentials and end web sessions from a clean device.

events.summary: Huntress reports two waves of attacks, on November 11 and 13, using ScreenConnect's Run Command feature to install rogue clients on 288 and then 205 hosts, apparently via a flawed third-party RMM+ extension. The SCKit toolkit tries to steal a technician's session cookie and replay it against the panel; Huntress has not seen that succeed. It names CVE-2026-84869 (fixed in 26.6.5) only as background, not as SCKit's method.
events.title: Huntress: rogue ScreenConnect clients pushed to hundreds of hosts in SCKit attacks; ConnectWise disables extensions

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Huntress report. ConnectWise's advisories page was then read in full: its newest entry is the Cloud Backup notice updated November 4, with no November notice on the ScreenConnect attacks; the separate security bulletins list did not render.

events.date_note: Two waves, November 11 and November 13; date is the latest wave. Huntress report published November 11.

review.note: Compared 288/48 and 205/41 hosts, dates, RMM+ 1.0.31/1.0.32, 26.6.5, no technician jump observed against Huntress and BleepingComputer; 400+ partner environments was about 400 in sources, now about 400

events.plain: Researchers disclosed 14 weaknesses in Copeland XWEB EVO devices that control commercial refrigeration. The maker no longer updates these devices, and VulnCheck saw attackers exploit two of the flaws on 12 and 13 November.

key_findings: VulnCheck disclosed 14 flaws, CVE-2026-124002 through CVE-2026-124015, in Dixell/Copeland XWEB EVO refrigeration supervisors including the 300D, 500D and 500 EVO.
They allow unauthenticated root command execution via the login page and a console script, and include a hardcoded administrator password and a daily password derivable from MAC address and date.
The EVO family is end of software support with no fixes after March 16, 2026; current firmware 5.8.8 is affected by several findings.
Internet scans show roughly 1,660 to 1,960 exposed EVO hosts.
Exploitation was seen for two flaws: config writes (CVE-2026-124014) from November 12 22:00 UTC and root execution probes (CVE-2026-124010) from November 13.
recommendations: Keep XWEB EVO devices off the public internet and segment them behind a VPN.
Plan migration to a supported platform, because firmware 5.8.8 will not be patched.
Hunt for the request patterns and source addresses VulnCheck published.

events.summary: VulnCheck disclosed 14 flaws in Dixell/Copeland XWEB EVO refrigeration supervisors, including unauthenticated root command execution on legacy builds and a computable administrator login code on firmware 5.8.8. events.action: Scan every open-weight model when it is brought in, before it runs. Flag undisclosed merged fine-tunes, test flagged models for hidden triggers, and decide to block, quarantine or approve on evidence rather than the model card.
events.exec: Downloaded AI models are third-party code; a cheap hidden backdoor is feasible, though so far shown only in the lab.
events.plain: CrowdStrike showed in the lab that freely shared AI models can carry hidden instructions that only switch on with a secret trigger, and described a way to check models before using them.

key_findings: Organisations that download open-weight models they cannot verify are at risk, most of all where agents run tool calls automatically.
A backdoored fine-tune behaves normally until a keyword or date triggers it; a cited demonstration cost about $50 to build.
Three backdoor classes are described: agent, code and safety (refusal removal).
In a lab test of 16 models the pipeline flagged all 8 backdoored ones and recovered a trigger for each.
Fine-tuning can weaken a model's refusals as a side effect even in adapters built for unrelated tasks.
recommendations: Scan every open-weight model statically when it is ingested.
Escalate flagged models to trigger recovery, using the static findings to choose which behaviour to test.
Decide before deployment whether to block, quarantine or approve each model on evidence, not its model card.
Treat open-weight models like any other third-party code.

events.summary: CrowdStrike published lab research on AI models that behave normally until a trigger word or date makes them act maliciously, for example by calling an attacker's address. It cites a demonstration that cost about $50 to build. Its two-stage method, weight comparison then trigger recovery, flagged all eight backdoored models in a 16-model test. No real-world cases are reported.
events.title: CrowdStrike shows how to detect backdoors hidden in open-weight AI model fine-tunes

events.exec: A supplier's leaked key led to tampered developer tools reaching up to 5,000 users; Cursor has dropped the supplier for inference.
events.plain: Coding-tool maker Cursor says a key it gave supplier Fireworks AI was exposed. Attackers used it to copy data, then posted harmful copies of a popular add-on for about 11 hours on October 29, reaching at most 5,000 users.

key_findings: An attacker used an access key Cursor had issued to Fireworks AI, which Fireworks exposed, to copy data from a read-only storage bucket.
The bucket held coding agent traces, mostly from 2025, from sessions not in Privacy Mode; under 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed.
Credentials in those traces opened some SaaS tools, archived non-production repositories, limited support data and usage metrics.
On October 29 malicious copies of the Claude Code extension, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, sat in the marketplace cache for about 11 hours; at most 5,000 users could have received them.
Cursor saw the last attacker activity on November 1 and moved all inference off Fireworks; Fireworks' own bulletin dates its first intrusion to August 3 to October 7.
recommendations: If you installed or updated to Claude Code extension 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 during the window, follow Cursor's October 30 security notice; uninstalling alone may not be enough.
Rotate any exposed keys; admins were sent lists of affected keys.
Fireworks customers: create new API keys, rotate third-party credentials named in your notice and review access logs for those credentials.

events.summary: Cursor's November 13 update says an access key it had issued to Fireworks AI was exposed by that supplier and used to copy coding agent traces from a read-only bucket. events.action: List every AK-SM800A reachable from the internet, including through integrators' 4G modems, and restrict management access to a VPN, private APN or strict IP whitelist. Put controllers on a separate OT network and change default passwords. Do not rely on patching alone.
events.exec: Refrigeration controllers under active attack have six more unfixed flaws; the researchers say only removing internet exposure helps.
events.impact: A joint US fact sheet of November 5 (CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, DoT) warns that actors altering refrigeration controller settings can force continuous heating and defrost cycles, causing inventory loss, fire hazard and loss of temperature visibility.
events.plain: Researchers found six unfixed weaknesses in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers that let outsiders take control without a password. Attack waves on such devices began in October, and Germany's BSI urges keeping them off the internet.

key_findings: Midnight Blue found six pre-authentication remote code execution flaws, stack-based buffer overflows, in Danfoss AK-SM800A firmware up to and including 5.3.2.
A further pre-authentication memory corruption bug sits in the controller's session control component.
CVE numbers are pending and technical details are withheld while coordinated disclosure with Danfoss continues.
Internet scans on November 10 showed hundreds of Danfoss systems exposed, plus over 1,000 Copeland and Dixell and hundreds of Eliwell controllers.
The attack waves began in France on October 11; public exploit code for older AK-SM800A flaws appeared within 48 hours.
recommendations: Inventory which controllers are internet-exposed, including through integrators' 4G modems.
Restrict management interfaces to a VPN, private APN or a highly restrictive firewall IP whitelist.
Do not treat patching or strict session control as sufficient; put effort into reducing exposure.
Treat IP whitelisting as an interim measure only.

events.title: Elastic: SANSAR Linux cryptominer fakes GPU readings to hide mining
events.actor: REF3364 (Elastic's tracking name; financially motivated, unattributed)
events.summary: Elastic Security Labs describes REF3364, a Linux cryptomining operation seen in late October 2026. Access came through an exposed Ray job agent. The toolkit, SANSAR, adds a kernel rootkit, a modified NVIDIA NVML wrapper that reports 0% GPU use and random temperatures, and an Ethereum-assisted backdoor. Elastic does not identify who is behind it.
events.plain: Attackers are secretly mining cryptocurrency on Linux servers with powerful graphics cards, and they fake the card's readings so the load looks normal.
events.exec: Hijacked AI compute raises costs and takes capacity from real workloads, and fake monitoring readings hide it.
events.action: Do not expose Ray job APIs to the internet, restrict who can submit jobs, and check hosts for a modified NVML library, unknown DKMS modules such as acpi_thermal_mgr and initramfs changes.

key_findings: Organisations running Linux GPU hosts for AI or ML work are the target; three hosts were hit in an intrusion tracked as REF3364 between 22 and 25 October 2026.
Initial access was an internet-reachable Ray job agent that accepted job submissions without authentication, followed by a reverse shell and an added SSH key.
The Rust orchestrator SANSAR takes commands over Tor, runs XMRig and SRBMiner-MULTI for mining, and can open shells and run a TCP SYN flood task.
A kernel rootkit (acpi_thermal_mgr.ko) hides selected processes, files and sockets, and a modified NVML library reports 0% GPU use with random temperature and power readings.
A separate netns backdoor gets its controller address from an Ethereum contract through public RPC and opens a shell on port 8080.
recommendations: Check who can submit jobs to GPU clusters and do not leave job agents such as Ray reachable without authentication.
Check whether GPU monitoring libraries such as NVML have been modified.

events.action: Inventory internet-facing apps and restrict admin, hypervisor and backup interfaces to private networks. Review ConnectWise-related Microsoft 365 app activity from October 1, 2026, rate-limit high-impact APIs, and rotate exposed secrets.
events.exec: Automated intrusions completing in hours shorten the time defenders have to detect and respond.
events.plain: The FBI warns that attackers are using ARTEX, a free AI-driven hacking tool, to break into organisations with little human effort, sometimes gaining high-level access in under three hours.

key_findings: Organisations worldwide in finance, government, technology, defence, semiconductors, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecoms and legal services are affected.
ARTEX turns plain-language goals into commands run by AI agents and relies on external LLM providers; attacker instances mostly use Chinese-origin models.
Some intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours; researchers counted over 1,600 exposed ARTEX consoles in early November 2026.
Entry came through ordinary web flaws (unsigned SAML assertions, injection, missing API authentication), weak or hardcoded admin credentials, stolen VPN configs and partner-tenant trust abuse.
A ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise led to attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 downstream tenants; a South Korean financial campaign took data on about 67,000 people.
recommendations: Inventory all internet-facing applications, including legacy and peripheral systems.
Restrict admin, SCM/Kudu, hypervisor and backup interfaces to trusted or private networks.
Apply least privilege to multi-tenant app permissions and monitor credential additions and high-privilege app-only activity.
Review ConnectWise-related activity from October 1, 2026 and keep affected connections disabled until ConnectWise issues restoration instructions.
Preserve Entra sign-in and audit logs before removing unauthorised credentials or grants.

It cites a South Korean financial campaign exposing about 67,000 people and a ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise with attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 downstream tenants.

events.action: Join calls through the official Zoom or Teams app with an invite code, keep the webcam off until the host is verified another way, never run scripts or paste code to fix audio, and enable MFA and login alerts on messaging accounts.
events.exec: A trusted contact on a video call can be a recording; crypto firms and open-source maintainers are the targets, with supply-chain risk for software users.
events.plain: The FBI says North Korean hackers stage fake video meetings using real recordings of earlier victims, then trick people into running a so-called fix that infects their computer and empties crypto wallets.

key_findings: Targets are cryptocurrency and Web3 workers, open-source developers and maintainers, and through them their contacts and employers' networks.
Operators take over a victim's messaging account, send contacts a look-alike meeting link and replay the victim's recorded webcam video in a staged session.
Posing as the contact, they claim an audio fault and have the target run an update or paste terminal code, installing a backdoor, keyloggers and a cookie harvester.
More than $400 million was stolen over roughly 18 months and the FBI seized over 900 victim webcam videos; one widely used JavaScript library was nearly compromised.
New elements are AI-generated deepfakes of known crypto figures, attempts on NPM and Rust maintainers, and theft delayed for months after compromise.
recommendations: Join meetings through the official Zoom or Teams app with an invite code rather than a web link.
Keep your camera off until you have verified the inviter, and confirm meetings through a different channel.
Never run scripts or paste code into a terminal to fix a meeting problem.
Enable multifactor authentication and login alerts on messaging accounts.
If compromised, move crypto to a new wallet with new seed phrases on a clean device and report to IC3 with the keyword FaceStealer.

events.summary: FBI FLASH AC-111226-MS (TLP:CLEAR) attributes the FaceStealer scheme to North Korean state-sponsored hackers (Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, BlueNoroff). They hijack a victim's messaging account, invite contacts to a counterfeit Zoom or Teams call, replay recorded webcam video and push a fake audio fix that installs malware. The FBI says over $400 million was stolen in about 18 months.

key_findings: Organisations in many sectors are affected, but the main focus is US legal professionals and legal technology decision makers; WordPress site operators are abused as infrastructure.
Attackers poison search results for low-competition, jurisdiction-specific legal phrases and serve a JavaScript loader from compromised WordPress sites behind a traffic filter.
The FBI counts over 1,000 infected WordPress sites as of October 2026, 216 administrator-controlled domains and more than $28 million in linked ransomware payments.
New in 2025-2026 are abuse of WordPress comment paths and use of geofencing and traffic distribution services.
Gootloader is treated as a ransomware precursor, with follow-on credential dumping, Kerberoasting, lateral movement over SMB and data exfiltration.
recommendations: Disable Windows Script Host where not needed, or control scripts with WDAC or AppLocker.
Block unapproved scripts and executables from user-writable locations and keep Defender, SmartScreen, AMSI and tamper protection enabled.
If the JavaScript file was opened, disconnect the device from the network and change credentials from a known-clean device.
Patch WordPress core, plugins and themes, require strong MFA for administrators and disable XML-RPC if unused.
Block PHP execution in wp-content/uploads and keep web and WAF logs off the web server.

key_findings: First incident, August 3 to October 7: an unauthorised party probed Fireworks systems and got in using stolen credentials and a vulnerability in one service.

Second incident, October 23 to 30: a third-party cloud provider hosting Fireworks development machines was itself breached, and the intruder ran an unauthorised workload.
The second incident exposed account and billing information, not card numbers, for all accounts created before October 30.
Fireworks says both incidents are contained; inference, the Training SDK and Nexus were not affected.
recommendations: Create new Fireworks API keys to replace revoked ones and update applications.
Rotate third-party credentials listed in your notice with their issuing providers; deleting the stored secret does not invalidate it.
Review access logs and data reachable with those credentials for unauthorised reads or changes.
Review API keys, users, evaluators, training jobs and datasets for unrecognised items and report them to Fireworks.

events.summary: Fireworks AI's November 17 bulletin describes two incidents. In the second, from October 23 to 30, a breach at a cloud provider hosting its development machines exposed account and billing information for every account created before October 30.

events.action: Telecom providers in Germany should prepare a process to receive and act on traffic-data preservation orders from the BfV and BND. Other firms with German operations should have legal teams read the final text once promulgated.
events.exec: German intelligence agencies gain offensive cyber and wider surveillance powers; telecom providers face new orders to preserve traffic data.
events.plain: Germany's parliament passed a law letting its foreign spy agency hack back against foreign attackers and giving its domestic agency wider surveillance powers, with an independent council approving orders in advance.

key_findings: The Bundestag adopted the bill in the committee's amended version by 308 to 190 with 71 abstentions; CDU/CSU and SPD backed it, AfD and Die Linke opposed.
The BND may act proactively against concrete threats from foreign powers, such as sabotaging attackers' systems or shutting down state hacker servers.
The BND may keep unreviewed content data up to six months and metadata up to twelve months.
The BfV gets limited covert intervention powers without coercion against persons, plus device access, biometric image matching and AI tools.
The Independent Control Council takes over prior review of orders and data protection oversight; a bill to strengthen parliamentary control is promised next year.
recommendations: Telecom providers must comply with preservation orders from the BfV and BND to freeze traffic data until disclosure conditions are met.
Agencies must obtain prior review of orders from the Independent Control Council and report to the Parliamentary Control Panel.

events.summary: The Bundestag passed the government's intelligence services reform on November 13 by 308 votes to 190 with 71 abstentions. The foreign service BND may act against concrete threats from foreign powers, for example by sabotaging attackers' systems or shutting down state hackers' servers. The domestic BfV gains narrower covert powers, device access, biometric image matching and AI analysis. Both can order telecom providers to freeze traffic data.

events.action: Search your GitHub organisations for wfx-docs branches and pull requests titled 'docs: dependency audit notes', and look for gaps in workflow run numbers. Where the payload ran, rotate every secret and cloud role those workflows could reach.
events.exec: Hijacked developer accounts are being used to plant key-stealing code in software projects, a risk for any team building on GitHub.
events.plain: Attackers used 4,837 taken-over GitHub accounts to probe more than 61,000 code projects and ran password-stealing code in the build systems of at least 1,835 of them.

key_findings: From about 12:45 UTC on November 10, 4,837 compromised GitHub accounts opened probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories to test for write access.
At least 1,835 repositories ran the payload and had credentials taken; the true figure may be higher because run logs were deleted.
The stealer arrives through an altered workflow, an npm postinstall hook or a throwaway workflow, and is reverted within about a minute.
It takes Actions secrets, cloud and registry credentials and AI provider keys, then pivots into AWS, GCP, Azure, Vault and Kubernetes.
New tricks include forged success status checks, rewritten AWS role trust policies and Azure federated credentials named wfx-ci for persistence.
recommendations: Search for wfx-docs branches and pull requests titled 'docs: dependency audit notes'.
Check for gaps in workflow run numbers, which may be the only trace of a run.
If the payload ran, rotate every secret and cloud role available to that repository's workflows.
Review AWS role trust policies and remove Azure federated credentials named wfx-ci.
Treat machines that installed the affected Packagist or Go module versions as compromised.

events.summary: Aikido reports that from November 10 an attacker used 4,837 compromised GitHub accounts to open probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories, then ran a secrets-stealing script in the build pipelines of at least 1,835. The script takes pipeline secrets and cloud credentials, pivots into cloud accounts and erases its traces within about a minute. One Packagist package and two Go module versions also carried it.
events.title: wfx-loot campaign uses 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts to push secrets-stealing malware

events.action: Shorten patch windows for internet-facing systems, check that monitoring can respond to fast automated activity, and follow the recommendations in Google's report. Patch PaperCut servers and LiteLLM gateways (CVE-2026-40217).
events.exec: Attackers are automating the discovery and exploitation of flaws, shrinking the time defenders have to apply fixes.
events.plain: Google's threat researchers reported on November 16 that criminal and suspected state-backed hackers are trying out AI tools that find and exploit weaknesses automatically.

key_findings: Several actors, financially motivated and suspected PRC-nexus espionage groups, are experimenting with agentic frameworks including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike AI and PentAGI.

CAIRN appeared in intrusions against targets including US aerospace; a customised PentAGI platform ran reconnaissance and scanning against organisations in Asia from late August to early October 2026.
For the first time Google saw vulnerability discovery and exploitation fully automated with no human involved, via an exploit_agent framework found on an exposed staging server.
Zero-day exploits averaged 8 a month in 2025 and 11 in 2026, with a spike to 22 in August 2026.
LLMJacking cases handled by Mandiant saw single-day fraudulent charges above $100,000 and cumulative abuse reaching $1 million before remediation; one route was LiteLLM flaw CVE-2026-40217.
recommendations: Use Mandiant's published hardening guide and defence framework for machine-speed, LLM-enabled offensive tooling.
Shorten patch windows, because LLMs are compressing the time from disclosure to working exploit.
Verify LLM-generated proof-of-concept exploits before acting on them; many published ones do not work.

events.summary: Google’s November 16 threat report says that, for the first time, it found actors using LLM frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation with no human in the loop. events.action: Apply Broadcom's fixed vCenter builds (8.0 U3m, 9.0.2.0200 or 9.1.1.0200) now; vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. Restrict inbound access to and egress from vCenter, following the hardening advice in Google's post.

attribution.claim: Suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221)

events.exec: A suspected state-backed group used an unpatched vCenter flaw to gain administrator access to virtualisation management; fixes exist for supported versions.
events.plain: Google says a suspected China-linked spy group exploited a previously unknown flaw in VMware vCenter to gain administrator access to virtual server management. Patches are out for supported versions.

key_findings: CVE-2026-123890 in vCenter Server is an unauthenticated SRP-6a session key disclosure over DCE/RPC leading to authentication bypass as administrator@vsphere.local; Broadcom patch page linked from the post.
The campaign used two zero-days in total; the other is the BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw CVE-2026-102764 from GTIG's 15 October post.
The actor moved from a BeyondTrust appliance to internal Linux appliances without EDR, then to vCenter and ESXi.
Five newly identified malware families and utilities are described, including the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, the BEARBONES backdoor, BONESAW and SAWSNAKE; LAZYBONES was also deployed.
The post names no victim organisations or countries.
recommendations: Apply the Broadcom patch immediately.
Use the Mandiant VCSA Hardening and Logging Tool after testing and change control.
Hunt with the YARA rules and indicators in the GTI collection.

events.action: Enforce FIDO2 security keys for admins, alert on new passkey or MFA device enrolments and tenant-wide exports, and when remediating revoke all sessions, tokens, OAuth grants and rogue passkeys, not just passwords.
events.actor: COLD RELIC (COLDRIVER, UNC4057, Star Blizzard, Callisto)
attack: T1114.002 Email Collection: Remote Email Collection
T1562.008 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Cloud Logs
events.exec: One cloud breach became a launchpad for the next: stolen contacts made phishing believable. Phishing-resistant MFA and full session revocation are key.
events.plain: Google says a Russian spy group stole one US organisation's staff lists and files, then pretended to be its employees to trick and break into a second organisation.

key_findings: In late 2025 COLD RELIC used stolen Super Admin credentials, an MFA push-fatigue attack and a residential proxy near the victim to enter a US organisation's cloud tenant.
It downloaded the whole cloud drive, exported staff lists, ran a tenant-wide Customer Takeout and deleted Alert Center notifications to hide the intrusion.
Unrevoked attacker-enrolled passkeys let it get back in after password and session resets.
In 2026 it impersonated an employee of the first victim over an encrypted messaging app to phish Entra ID credentials at a second US organisation, then bulk-downloaded files.
GTIG observed new COLD RELIC phishing operations as recently as November 2026.
recommendations: Use phishing-resistant FIDO2/WebAuthn MFA and restrict and audit passkey and MFA device registrations.
Revoke all sessions, refresh tokens, OAuth grants, passkeys and backup codes when remediating, not just passwords.
Block or alert on admin logons from residential proxies and consumer ISPs.
Apply DLP rules to cloud storage for credentials, rosters and .pst files, and alert on tenant-wide exports and directory downloads.

events.summary: Mandiant and GTIG describe two linked intrusions by Russian espionage group COLD RELIC. In late 2025 it used a stolen Super Admin password and MFA fatigue to take a US organisation's entire cloud drive and staff directory. In 2026 it impersonated that organisation's staff over a messaging app to phish a second US organisation through Entra ID. GTIG saw new COLD RELIC phishing as recently as November 2026.
events.title: Google: Russia's COLD RELIC used data stolen from one US organisation to breach a second

validation.note: Reviewed against the full original Google Cloud threat intelligence post.

review.note: Two-intrusion account, Super Admin plus MFA fatigue, Entra ID phish, Nov 2026 phishing against Google post dated Nov 17

events.action: Patch internet-facing web applications and WordPress plugins promptly after release and review web server logs for webshells and unexpected file changes.
events.actor: Unattributed; Google notes Russian-language comments in the framework's configuration

events.exec: The gap between a patch release and working attacks is shrinking; patch internet-facing web software faster.

events.plain: Google says attackers built an AI tool that reads software security fixes, writes attacks from them and launches them with no person involved. It was aimed at French websites.

report.doc_id: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
key_findings: GTIG found an exposed staging server hosting exploit_agent, a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that integrates with several frontier and local LLMs.
The framework continuously compares code before and after patch announcements, drafts exploits and executes them without human intervention.
The server also held scripts for internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells and removing other attackers' webshells.
Victim telemetry suggests interest in French media and entertainment websites and the education sector; a configuration comment is written in Russian.
GTIG says threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs on patched n-day flaws than to hunt zero-days.
recommendations: Verify LLM-generated proof-of-concept exploits before relying on them, since many published ones do not work.

events.summary: Google's November 16 AI Threat Tracker says it found an exposed staging server running exploit_agent, a multi-agent framework tied to several language models that compares popular web application code before and after patches, drafts exploits and runs them without a human. Victim data on the server suggests the operator targeted French media, entertainment and education sites. Google says this is the first time it has seen fully automated discovery and exploitation.
events.title: Google: autonomous exploit_agent framework turned patches into exploits, aimed at French websites

validation.note: Original Google report read in full; The Hacker News and SiliconANGLE read. 'Russian-speaking' is Google's inference from a Russian-language comment, not an attribution; no government role is stated.

review.note: exploit_agent description, French targets, Russian-language comments not attribution, against Google report

events.action: Development teams, especially in crypto: review .claude/settings.json files in repositories for commands you did not add, treat changes to them like code changes, audit GitHub access tokens with Copilot-style names, and warn staff not to run fix scripts from meeting pages.
events.exec: Developer tool configuration files are being abused for persistent access at crypto firms; treat them as code.
events.plain: Google says suspected North Korean hackers tricked staff at cryptocurrency firms into running harmful commands, then altered a settings file in code projects so that opening an AI coding tool installed a hidden backdoor.

key_findings: Google describes recent intrusions against cryptocurrency organisations in North America and Europe by a suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE cluster it links to North Korea.
Fake recruiter profiles with AI-generated images steered targets to bogus meeting platforms, where ClickFix prompts had them run fix scripts that were likely LLM-written.
Inside victim networks the actor edited .claude/settings.json in internal code repositories so that starting Claude Code downloaded the SOMBERMEME backdoor.
The actor created GitHub personal access tokens named after Microsoft Copilot to disguise lateral movement.
Google frames this as abuse of native AI agent execution hooks and an internal supply chain vector; the post gives no indicator list.
recommendations: The post gives no step-by-step guidance for this activity; it points to Mandiant's hardening guide for machine-speed, LLM-enabled tooling.
Verify LLM-generated proof-of-concept exploits before relying on them, since many published ones do not work.

events.summary: Google's November 16 AI Threat Tracker says a suspected North Korean cluster, MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE, used fake recruiter profiles and ClickFix lures against cryptocurrency organisations in North America and Europe. After getting in, it edited .claude/settings.json files in internal code repositories so that starting Claude Code downloaded the SOMBERMEME backdoor. The post does not say whether this is a product flaw and lists no indicators.
events.title: Google: North Korean actor backdoors crypto developers through Claude Code settings files

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Google Threat Intelligence Group document.

events.action: Review which third-party providers and cloud systems hold your data, limit what their accounts can search and export, and delete data you no longer need. Report incidents to the HKCERT hotline on (852) 8105 6060.
events.exec: Hong Kong's CERT says recent breaches at a travel firm, a university and a retail group show third-party and cloud systems are entry points for large data leaks.
events.plain: Hong Kong's cyber emergency team warns that several recent data leaks at local organisations show that data held by third-party providers and cloud services is at risk. It asks organisations to hold less data and limit access to it.

key_findings: HKCERT cites recent incidents in travel, education and retail: unauthorised access to the back-end system of EGL Tours' third-party IT provider, a Hong Kong Metropolitan University incident that may have involved about 5,000 people, and an A.S. Watson Group incident involving a third-party supplier.

It urges collecting and keeping only required data, restricting account, system and provider access to data (least privilege, with care over bulk export), and proportionate safeguards such as encryption.
recommendations: Collect and retain only necessary data and delete or anonymise the rest.
Restrict data access permissions for accounts, systems and third-party providers.
Apply safeguards in proportion to data sensitivity, including encryption at rest and in transit.

Huntress recommends updating every technician's host client to 26.6.5 or later.
recommendations: Update technician host clients to 26.6.5 or later.
If you cannot patch, remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups.

Monitor and audit systems to detect suspicious access.

Investigate suspected cases promptly, keep affected people informed and act where wrongdoing is found.

events.title: Kaspersky: AuditTeam ransomware crew uses OpsAgent framework and a signed driver to kill security tools
events.summary: Kaspersky describes AuditTeam, a ransomware-linked group that frames its demand as an audit and consulting fee and uses the OpsAgent framework, in C++ and Rust versions. Activity runs from January to October 2026, with infections in seven countries and its leak site claiming victims in seven further countries. It kills security tools using a signed Beijing Jiangmin driver.
events.plain: Researchers describe a ransomware group that disguises extortion as a consulting bill and switches off antivirus using a legitimately signed driver.

events.action: Check systems against Kaspersky's published hashes, domains, IP address and file paths (such as syscache.dat and kvcore.sys); the report says shared CloudFront IPs are not reliable indicators on their own.

key_findings: Kaspersky says AuditTeam infected dozens of organisations, with victims seen in China, the Philippines, Senegal, Italy, Finland, Hong Kong and Russia, and its leak site lists victims in seven further countries.

The OpsAgent framework gives the operators file system management, process injection, privilege escalation, keylogging, screenshot capture and network pivoting, and the ransom note demands an "Audit & Consulting fee" for a vulnerability report.
The campaign began in January 2026 and was active through October 2026 at a minimum; the page does not state how the group gets in.
OpsAgent was moved from C++ to Rust, and the Rust version uses CloudFront subdomains as C2 endpoints found through a GitHub repository.
An AV/EDR killer installs a driver disguised as a Beijing Jiangmin product and works from a kill list of about 220 process names.
recommendations: Check systems against the published stager and driver hashes, the two CloudFront domains, the IP address and the file paths such as syscache.dat and kvcore.sys.
Do not rely on the shared CloudFront IP addresses alone as indicators; the report says they cannot serve as reliable standalone IOCs.

events.title: Kaspersky: Retadup worm's revived servers now deliver CoffeeLoader
events.summary: Kaspersky says servers once used by the Retadup USB worm, disrupted by French police in 2019, now serve a new CoffeeLoader variant. The loader hides in a patched 7-Zip library and uses a packer that runs decryption on the GPU. Kaspersky says its products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems this year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, and it is unclear who runs the servers.
events.plain: An old USB worm that police shut down in 2019 is back and installing a newer malware loader that can bring in further malware. Kaspersky blocked infection attempts on about 15,000 systems.
events.exec: Removable drives can still carry malware that opens the door to later attacks, including from long-dead botnets.
events.action: Block autorun and restrict USB storage on endpoints, scan removable drives, and hunt for a patched 7z.dll running via rundll32.exe from %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%.

key_findings: A new CoffeeLoader variant uses a patched 7z.dll carrying a new version of the Armoury packer, which runs decryption on the GPU via OpenGL instead of OpenCL.
Domains used as Retadup command servers were re-registered about two years ago and first served SmokeLoader, then CoffeeLoader from early 2025.

Kaspersky products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems in the first three quarters of the year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, far fewer than the 850,000 machines disinfected in 2019.
It is unclear whether the worm's author or another actor revived the servers.

events.action: Treat any unapproved remote-management tool such as a MeshCentral agent as suspicious, review servers for unexpected GitHub, Microsoft Graph, SharePoint or Ably traffic, and load Kaspersky's published indicators into detection.
events.exec: Espionage tools are hiding inside traffic to trusted cloud services, making them harder to spot with normal network filtering.
events.org: Government bodies in Asia and Africa
events.plain: Kaspersky described a spying campaign on government networks in Asia and Africa. Hidden access tools take their orders through GitHub, SharePoint and a messaging service, so the traffic looks like normal cloud use.

key_findings: Victims are in Asia and Africa, mainly government; the worked example is two MeshCentral agent instances inside a Taiwanese organisation.
The entry point is unknown; evidence suggests reuse of an earlier infection, after which the MeshCentral agent was used for DLL sideloading and payload drops.
GitDoor receives commands and uploads results through GitHub accounts created between September 2024 and December 2025, and loads plug-ins and shellcode.
GraphDoor authenticates to Microsoft Graph, keeps encrypted victim data in SharePoint and loads plug-ins for keylogging, screenshots and proxy tunnels over Ably.
Kaspersky sees overlaps with Chinese-speaking FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle but says it cannot definitively attribute the activity.
recommendations: Treat the appearance of legitimate remote-management tools in the environment as suspicious.
Do not rely on network detection alone, since command traffic goes to trusted cloud APIs.
Use the indicators Kaspersky publishes in both parts for hunting.

events.summary: Kaspersky's two-part report describes Operation ShadowCloud, found in early 2026, against mainly government networks in Asia and Africa. Attackers abused a MeshCentral agent to sideload loaders that run GitDoor, which takes commands through GitHub, and GraphDoor, which uses Microsoft Graph and SharePoint. Plug-ins add keylogging, screenshots and proxies over the Ably messaging service. Kaspersky notes overlaps with Chinese-speaking groups but makes no firm attribution.

events.title: Linux KVM flaw CVE-2026-99312 affects AMD hosts with nested virtualization
events.geo_basis: software flaw with no single location
events.summary: The Linux kernel CVE team published CVE-2026-99312 on 18 November: when INIT is emulated with nested SVM active on AMD, KVM can run with a stale MMU context. DigitalOcean calls it a guest-to-host escape and says a researcher read about 127 GB of host RAM (read-only). It is fixed in kernels 7.3.5, 6.18.64 and 6.12.118; Red Hat rates it Moderate.
events.plain: A bug in Linux's virtualization code on AMD servers with nested virtualization could let someone with root in a virtual machine read the host's memory. Fixed kernel versions are out.
events.exec: Hosting providers on AMD with nested virtualization could expose host memory to a tenant until kernels are updated.
events.action: Update to a fixed kernel (7.3.5, 6.18.64 or 6.12.118), or as DigitalOcean advises set the kvm_amd nested parameter to 0 until you can.
events.impact: Scores differ: Red Hat gives a preliminary CVSS 3.1 of 5.6 (Moderate); the cve.org record shows 8.8. Red Hat says Intel-based KVM is not affected. Per The Hacker News, citing VirtFusion, no use outside research was reported and no exploit code was published.

validation.note: Kernel CVE announcement, DigitalOcean and Red Hat pages read; The Hacker News adds context. DigitalOcean and the kernel text describe the impact differently (memory access vs. stale MMU context); Red Hat frames it as DoS or memory corruption.

review.note: Compared with kernel CVE announcement (18 Nov), DigitalOcean (19 Nov), Red Hat, THN. Summary said fixes shipped 17 Nov and 'read and modify' memory: neither found in sources. Now: published 18 Nov, DigitalOcean's guest-to-host escape with about 127 GB read-only, fixed 7.3.5/6.18.64/6.12.118, Red Hat

events.title: Study of 428 LLM API routers finds some inject malicious code and steal credentials
events.date_note: Date of the ITmedia report; the paper itself was submitted to arXiv on 9 April 2026.
events.summary: A paper by researchers at UC Santa Barbara and other institutions measured 428 third-party LLM API routers, 28 paid and 400 free. One paid and eight free routers actively injected malicious code, 17 routers touched researcher-owned AWS canary credentials, and one drained ETH from a researcher-owned private key.
events.plain: Researchers found that some middleman services connecting AI coding agents to AI models altered commands, and some touched or drained decoy keys.
events.exec: Routing AI agent traffic through unvetted third parties exposes API keys, cloud credentials and code to theft or tampering.
events.action: Send agent traffic only to the model provider or a router you operate and trust, and rotate any keys that passed through an unvetted router.
events.impact: 9 of 428 routers injected code; 17 routers touched AWS canary credentials; one drained ETH from a researcher-owned key.

sources.name: arXiv: Your Agent Is Mine: Measuring Malicious Intermediary Attacks on the LLM Supply Chain

key_findings: The study scanned 428 routers, 28 paid and 400 free, and found one paid and eight free routers actively injecting malicious code.
Two routers used adaptive triggers such as waiting for 50 prior calls, limiting payloads to YOLO-mode sessions, or targeting only Rust and Go projects.
17 routers touched researcher-owned AWS canary credentials and one drained ETH from a researcher-owned private key.
Poisoning studies with a deliberately leaked OpenAI key and weakly configured decoys showed the routers' traffic exposed 99 credentials across 440 Codex sessions.
report.publisher: UC Santa Barbara and co-authors (arXiv paper)
recommendations: Use client-side mitigations such as a fail-closed policy gate, response-side anomaly screening and append-only transparency logging, which the paper says reduce exposure today.
Press for provider-backed response integrity, which the paper says is ultimately needed to secure the ecosystem.

validation.note: The paper's arXiv abstract and the start of its HTML text were read; ITmedia reports the same figures but words the AWS result more strongly ("misused"), so the paper's wording is used.

review.note: Paper abstract says 17 routers touched AWS canary credentials without saying free; only ITmedia says free. Removed 'free' from summary, impact, key finding. Counts 428/28/400, 1 paid + 8 free injecting, ETH checked against abstract and ITmedia.

events.summary: Luxor Technology confirmed that from about 6 pm Pacific on 14 November an intruder used its Commander fleet-management platform to redirect hashrate from just over a dozen client accounts to the OCEAN pool. Luxor says it patched the flaw within two hours, restored settings, found no data exfiltrated, and will compensate clients and publish a post-mortem. Its CEO blamed an AI-enabled attack; the method is undisclosed.
events.title: Luxor Commander mining software hijacked to redirect clients' bitcoin hashrate

validation.note: The Cyber Express and CryptoSlate both report Luxor's own statements. The 64,000-machine and 13 EH/s scale is a third-party estimate (GalaxyMind) that Luxor has not confirmed; Luxor says just over a dozen accounts. The attack method and the AI-enabled claim come from Luxor's CEO and are unverified.

review.note: Compared with Cyber Express and CryptoSlate: 6pm PT 14 Nov, over a dozen accounts, patched in 2h, no exfiltration, CEO AI claim and scale estimate caveated

events.action: Data-centre operators and their customers in Malaysia: follow the Digital Infrastructure (Data Centres) Bill ahead of tabling in 2027 and map current security, disaster recovery and business continuity arrangements against an all-hazards standard. No action is required yet.
events.exec: Data centres in Malaysia are set to be regulated as critical national infrastructure, with new security and resilience duties.
events.plain: Malaysia's digital minister said a proposed law setting security, reliability and management rules for data centres is in final drafting and will go to parliament next year.

key_findings: In a written reply to Parliament dated November 12 the ministry said study of the draft Digital Infrastructure (Data Centres) Bill is in its final stages.
The bill is to be tabled in 2027 and would give a clearer framework for data-centre protection, operational resilience and governance.
It takes an all-hazards approach: cyber threats, system failures, operational disruption, natural disasters and physical and supply chain risks.
The ministry cites ICT and e-commerce at 23.5 per cent of GDP in 2025 and RM385.71 billion of approved digital investment from 2021 to June 2026.
recommendations: Once in force, data-centre operators would have to meet standards on security, resilience and operational continuity coordinated by the ministry.
Operators should expect requirements on preparedness, disaster recovery and business continuity.

events.summary: Malaysia's Digital Ministry said in a parliamentary written reply dated November 12 that study of the draft Digital Infrastructure (Data Centres) Bill is in its final stages and the bill will be tabled in 2027. The framework would take an all-hazards approach covering cyber threats, system failures, natural disasters and physical and supply chain risks, with standards on security, resilience, continuity and disaster recovery. No bill text is public.
events.title: Malaysia to table data-centre security bill next year

events.exec: AI coding agents widen what a phished sign-in can reach, including code, past sessions and local commands; restrict agent session and memory settings.
events.plain: Microsoft tested how tricking a developer into typing a sign-in code could let a hacker control their AI coding assistant and read their private code. It has not seen this used in real attacks yet.

key_findings: In a controlled simulation, a test account approved a GitHub device-code request started by an attacker-controlled client using the public Copilot CLI client ID.
With that approval researchers could steer a remote-control-enabled Copilot CLI session to run a command, add misleading memory entries, read synced sessions and access private repositories.
The requested scopes included repo, read:user, read:org, gist and codespace, chosen by the client that starts the flow.
The technique applies to any public client supporting the device flow; Microsoft has not observed these four outcomes in the wild.
Microsoft cites earlier device-code phishing campaigns including Storm-2372 and EvilTokens, which it helped disrupt in September 2026.
recommendations: Approve device codes only for sign-ins you started yourself, even on the genuine github.com page.
Review GitHub Copilot CLI session storage and remote-control policy and choose the least permissive setting.
Review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorisations and limit repository access by role.
Review Copilot Memory for suspicious entries, and connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Defender for Cloud Apps for visibility.

events.summary: Microsoft researchers showed in a lab that a phished GitHub device-code approval for the Copilot CLI client could let an attacker steer a remotely controllable agent session, plant misleading memory entries, read cloud-synced sessions and reach private repositories. These are proof-of-concept results, not attacks seen in the wild. Microsoft added two Defender XDR detections for the email and Teams lures.
events.title: Microsoft: one phished device-code approval could let attackers steer AI coding agents

key_findings: Microsoft observed a high-volume phishing campaign on November 13 aimed at organisations in multiple sectors worldwide.
Emails use subjects like 'Outage' plus a random token and sender names posing as service-health notices, claiming four messages were held after a November 12 Exchange Online incident.
A 'RESTORE MESSAGES' button leads to a likely credential-phishing page; Microsoft has not confirmed credential capture.
Randomised subjects, recipient-specific tracking links and rotating sender domains are used to defeat simple pattern matching.
Microsoft has not attributed the campaign to a named actor or malware family.
recommendations: Search mail telemetry for the published sender domains, subject patterns and lure phrases, then quarantine and remove delivered copies.
Identify users who clicked using click, proxy and endpoint logs.
For anyone who may have entered credentials, reset the password, revoke sessions and tokens, verify MFA registrations and review inbox rules and OAuth grants.
Turn on Safe Links, Safe Attachments and zero-hour auto purge, and prefer phishing-resistant MFA.
Remind users that genuine service-health notices do not point to non-Microsoft sites; check the Microsoft 365 admin center.

events.action: Update Linux kernels to 6.12.117, 6.18.63, 7.3.4 or your distribution's fixed package, internet-facing servers first. Until then, disable SYN cookies in every network namespace or force a single receive queue with RPS and RFS off.
events.exec: A remote crash flaw in Linux servers (kernels since 2015) that use multiple receive queues or RPS; fixes exist and internet-facing systems should be updated first.
events.plain: A flaw called NoisyTCP lets outsiders crash Linux servers over the network without logging in. It has been in Linux since 2015. Fixed versions are out.

key_findings: NoisyTCP is a race in the kernel's lockless TCP established-socket lookup that can return a reused, unhashed socket with no listener, causing a NULL dereference and kernel panic.
It is remote and needs no authentication against plain TCP listeners such as Nginx, Apache and SSH in default configurations; in a container the panic takes down the whole host.
The bug dates from a 2015 commit (kernel 4.4) and was fixed upstream on November 3, 2026; stable fixes are 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4.
It needs two or more receive queues or RPS; the researcher reports about 5 seconds to 2 minutes on virtual machines and about 14 hours on a quiet 8-queue bare-metal server.
A second flow can cause a remote use-after-free but is described as hard to trigger; the CVE record's CISA-added score is 5.9 with exploitation marked none.
report.publisher: Hyunwoo Kim (researcher disclosure on oss-security) and the Linux kernel CVE team
recommendations: Apply the kernel fix (commit 4e2b3ef19e0e, shipped in 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4) as the priority.
As a temporary measure, disable SYN cookies (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0) in every network namespace, accepting weaker SYN-flood protection.
Alternatively, serialise to a single receive queue and disable RPS and RFS on interfaces receiving external traffic.

events.summary: Researcher Hyunwoo Kim disclosed NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288) on November 15 after a distribution embargo ended. A race in the Linux kernel's TCP socket lookup lets a remote, unauthenticated sender panic servers running ordinary TCP services; in containers the whole host goes down. The flaw dates to 2015; fixed in kernels 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4. A poster says 5.15.225 lacks the fix; 5.15.226-rc1 has it.
events.title: NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288): 11-year-old Linux kernel TCP race lets remote attackers crash servers

events.action: Inventory every Java runtime, including bundled ones, and install the fixed releases (for example 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1), internet-facing systems first. See Rapid7's advisory for compensating controls where patching is not possible.

events.plain: Security firm Rapid7 and the US cyber agency warned of a serious flaw in recent versions of Java that could let outsiders run their own code. Oracle has released fixes.

key_findings: Memory corruption in the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot JVM; specially crafted input could allow unauthenticated remote code execution (CISA).
OpenJDK lists releases 17, 21, 25 and 27 as affected; Oracle fixed versions include 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1.

Rapid7 gives Oracle's CVSS v3.1 score as 8.1 (High); neither Rapid7 nor CISA reports exploitation in the wild. SecurityWeek (Nov 19) reports attempts: GreyNoise saw over 150 requests from five IP addresses and no successful intrusions on its sensors; Previdian logged nine attempts from six IPs and says its data cannot confirm compromise.
Researchers at Calif demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against several Java applications; Rapid7 says a reliable exploit needs significant extra work.
recommendations: Apply Oracle's November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update or the OpenJDK fixed releases, internet-facing systems first.
Inventory all JDKs and Java runtimes, including bundled ones; use compensating controls such as Base64 input validation where patching is not possible.

events.summary: Rapid7 and CISA warn of CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell), a memory corruption bug in the x86-64 HotSpot JVM Base64 decoder that could allow remote code execution; Oracle released fixes on November 17. SecurityWeek (Nov 19) reports GreyNoise saw over 150 matching requests from five IP addresses, with no successful intrusions seen on its sensors; Cisco, Siemens, Elastic and Red Hat issued advisories.

events.action: Upgrade React and Next.js to fixed versions; until then strip or reject the x-middleware-subrequest header at the proxy or WAF, check logs for it and for /_next/image requests aimed at the metadata address, rotate every secret the server could reach, and enforce IMDSv2.
attack: T1552.005 Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
events.date_note: Date of OpenSourceMalware's published research; the repositories were created in waves from October 22.
